title: Bill Russell's Celtics
text:
In 1956 Boston Celtics coach Red Auerbach made a trade to acquire the draft rights to Bill Russell, a center from the University of San Francisco who scored relatively little but defended, blocked shots and rebounded like no one before him.

Russell did not try to be the team's top scorer. He blocked shots so that they stayed in play and went to a teammate, rebounded and fired outlet passes to start fast breaks, and covered for teammates who gambled on defense. The Celtics built their game around him and around passing and unselfish play. Auerbach gave players clear roles and rarely cared who scored the points.

The results have no equal in North American team sports. In Russell's thirteen seasons, from 1957 to 1969, the Celtics won eleven championships, including eight in a row. In 1966 Auerbach stepped down and Russell became player-coach, the first Black head coach in the NBA, and he won two more titles in that double role before retiring.

Russell was famously nervous before big games, sometimes sick before going on court. He also faced racist abuse in Boston itself. In his memoir Second Wind he wrote about rare moments when the play rose to a level where the whole team seemed to move as one and even the opponents raised their game, and said those moments mattered to him more than the trophies.
lesson: The most valuable team member is often the one who makes everyone else better, not the one with the most points. Measure contributions by what the team achieves.
source: NBA records; Bill Russell and Taylor Branch, Second Wind: The Memoirs of an Opinionated Man (1979)
